clinicalPearls: A compulsive hair-pulling disorder producing irregular, often bizarre patches of incomplete hair loss with hairs broken at varying lengths within the same area
Classically affects easily reachable areas, so the tonsure or Friar Tuck pattern spares the occiput and peripheries that are harder to grasp
Eyebrows and eyelashes may also be plucked, and ingestion of pulled hair (trichophagia) can rarely form a gastric trichobezoar, described in Rapunzel syndrome
Trichoscopy shows broken hairs of differing lengths, coiled hairs, flame hairs, V-signs and hair powder, with preserved follicular ostia
The hair-pull test is negative in pulled areas and the follicular ostia remain intact, confirming a non-scarring mechanical cause
It is more common in children and adolescents and is often associated with anxiety, obsessive-compulsive traits or psychosocial stress
Habit-reversal training and psychological therapy are first-line, and because the process is non-scarring hair regrows once pulling stops, though very prolonged traction may eventually scar
reference.pathophysiology: Trichotillomania is a body-focused repetitive behaviour in which recurrent pulling, twisting or plucking of hair produces mechanical breakage of shafts and traumatic disruption of follicles. It is classified among the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders and often serves to relieve tension or anxiety. Because the follicles are mechanically injured rather than inflamed or destroyed, the ostia are preserved and regrowth occurs once the behaviour ceases, although very prolonged or forceful pulling can occasionally cause permanent follicular damage and secondary scarring.
additionalDifferentials: Alopecia areata, with smooth patches, exclamation-mark hairs and a positive pull test at margins
Tinea capitis, with scaling, broken hairs and positive mycology
Traction alopecia, which is marginal and tension-related
additionalInvestigations: Trichoscopy to identify broken hairs of varying length, flame hairs and V-signs
Mycological examination to exclude tinea capitis
Scalp biopsy in equivocal cases showing pigment casts, trichomalacia and empty follicles without significant inflammation
Psychological or psychiatric assessment for comorbid anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder
Abdominal imaging if trichophagia with a bezoar is suspected
redFlags: Abdominal pain, a palpable mass or obstruction suggesting a trichobezoar (Rapunzel syndrome)
Signs of significant underlying psychiatric distress or self-harm
Loss of follicular ostia indicating secondary scarring from very prolonged pulling
reference.prognosis: In young children the behaviour is frequently transient and resolves with reassurance and simple behavioural measures; in adolescents and adults it tends to be more chronic and relapsing, but the alopecia is reversible unless prolonged trauma has caused scarring.
pitfalls: Mistaking the bizarre incomplete patches for alopecia areata and missing the behavioural cause
Overlooking trichophagia and the risk of a gastric bezoar
Confronting the patient or family unsympathetically, undermining engagement with behavioural therapy
Attributing failure of regrowth to the diagnosis rather than considering secondary scarring
management: Use behavioural therapy as first-line treatment, principally habit-reversal training and cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the body-focused repetitive behaviour
Consider pharmacological adjuncts such as N-acetylcysteine, or an SSRI or clomipramine where there is comorbid anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder, recognising the evidence is modest
Identify and treat comorbid anxiety, depression or obsessive-compulsive disorder that drive the pulling
Apply simple stimulus-control and barrier measures, and offer reassurance and watchful support in young children in whom the behaviour is often transient
Screen for trichophagia and investigate for a gastric trichobezoar with abdominal imaging, arranging endoscopic or surgical removal if the Rapunzel syndrome is present
Refer to psychology or psychiatry for structured therapy and provide family support
Follow up for relapse, as adolescent and adult disease tends to be chronic and remitting
